opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's probably the part of my week I protect most fiercely. On any given day I'm bouncing between research discussions, product questions, fundraising, the operational stuff that comes with running a young company. But when I sit down with someone who might join Axiom, it pulls me back to first principles. Why are we doing this? Why does building an AI mathematician matter right now? Every time I explain it to a new person, I have to articulate it fresh, and that keeps me honest.

The other side is that at our stage, the people *are* the company. A small team trying to do formal reasoning, theorem proving, Lean, large-scale model training. These are rare combinations of skills. One great mathematician who also deeply understands machine learning can change our trajectory. So I don't treat recruiting as an HR function I delegate. I think of it as maybe the highest-leverage thing I do as a founder.

And it's genuinely fun. A lot of the people we talk to are former olympiad kids, researchers who left a PhD halfway, engineers who secretly love number theory. The conversations often turn into us just doing math together, arguing about whether some conjecture is within reach of automated proof in five years. Those are the moments I remember why I started this. It doesn't feel like selling; it feels like finding the people who were already thinking about the same dream, and telling them, hey, there's a place where we're actually building it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's one of the few parts of my day that I actually protect. Running Axiom means most of my hours get eaten by things that are urgent but not necessarily energizing: fundraising conversations, infrastructure decisions, making sure the training runs don't fall over at two in the morning. Recruiting is different. When I sit down with someone who might join us, I have to re-articulate from scratch why we're doing this, and that's clarifying for me, not just for them.

Our mission is a strange one to explain. We're trying to build an AI that does real mathematics, that proves theorems, that can eventually contribute to the frontier of the field rather than just pass exams. Most people who are good enough to work on this have a lot of options. They could go to a big lab, they could stay in academia, they could start their own thing. So I'm not really selling them a job. I'm trying to find out whether they have the same itch I have, that sense that mathematics is the right proving ground for whether these systems can actually reason, and that getting it right matters beyond math itself.

What I've noticed is that the best conversations don't feel like interviews. They turn into working sessions. Someone will push back on how we're thinking about formalization, or ask why we care about Lean rather than natural-language proofs, and twenty minutes later we're at a whiteboard arguing. Those are the people I want. I've learned more about weaknesses in our own roadmap from candidates than from almost anyone else, because they come in without our assumptions baked in.

There's also something personal in it. I came to this from pure math, and I remember how hard it was to decide to leave that path, how much it felt like a betrayal of something. So when I talk with a postdoc or a grad student who's wrestling with the same question, I take it seriously. I'm not trying to convince everyone. Sometimes the right answer for them is to stay and prove theorems the old way, and I'll tell them that. But when it clicks, when someone realizes they can bring the thing they love into this new form, that's the moment that makes the rest of the week worth it.
